questions.text: Find uncommon words from two strings, given the full sentence string separately.
Maximizing the OR value in an array, given you can multiply any element by 2, at most k times.

rounds.description: Resume discussion focusing on GenAI project, vector databases in LangChain, cosine similarity, static/dynamic components in React, and knowledge about MSCI.

questions.text: Explain how vector databases work in LangChain and what cosine similarity is.
Explain static and dynamic components in React.

Given Products(pid, …) and Orders(pid, oid), find unsold products using LEFT JOIN where oid is NULL.

rounds.name: HR Round

questions.text: Introduce yourself professionally.
Difference between ML and Data Science and your interest.
Family background.
Do you know about MSCI? How do you know about it?

Willingness to relocate / preferred location.

tips.text: Even if you are not super good at DSA, practice standard problems from Striver's SDE sheet or do daily LeetCode to solve at least medium questions comfortably.
Practice and complete the LeetCode SQL 50 a week before or during placement for decent SQL experience.
For System Design, refer to Piyush Garg (https://www.youtube.com/@piyushgargdev) and Arpit Bhayani (https://www.youtube.com/@AsliEngineering) on YouTube.
For core subjects, explore different videos or GFG articles, and clarify doubts using GPT/Gemini; good resources include GateSmashers (https://www.youtube.com/@GateSmashers) and Arpit Bhayani.
Prepare your introduction and general HR questions or project descriptions in written form; you can use AI tools to enhance this.
Read all interview experiences of the particular company before interviews to get an idea of question variety.
Luck can play a part; focus on presenting one‑liners about projects to steer interviews toward your strengths.
Do not juggle between two companies; stay focused on one and prepare for it.
Do not be demotivated if rejected; keep preparing and applying to other companies.
Feel free to connect on LinkedIn for help: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aroosh-joshi-59601524b/

rounds.name: OA
rounds.description: a coding test, 75 minutes in duration. There were 2 coding/DSA problems and an SQL problem.

questions.text: There’s a keypad. Each key takes a certain amount of time to press every time you press it. Input is a list of integer pairs like [[0,2], [1,6], [3,8], [2, 4], …]. Here, [0,2] means ‘a’ took 2 seconds to be pressed and so on. So all letters (keys) are 0 indexed starting from ‘a’. The output should be the letter of the key that had the maximum pressing time.

Input is a string. This string’s various substrings contain multiple permutations of the word “programmer” as subsequences. The task is to find the number of letters between the first and last such substring.

Given 2 tables, States, and Votes. The Votes table has the votername, state voted for. Return, for each state, a comma separated concatenated string of name of voter, and number of votes given, in the same cell.

tips.text: Brute force almost always works.
every minute is valuable. Code up the brute force, see if it runs. Probably will.
don’t get intimidated by how many leet problems other people have done. On-campus OA’s are easy.

If you have a year before placements: do give as many cf contests as you can. They teach you how to think. I;m not saying rank push. But get yourself to a spot where you can solve div 2 A and B always, and C at least half the time.

Or if you have very few months before placements and you don’t have a single leet problem. Do top interview 150, then some 10-20 random medium/hards, and you’re good to go tbh. But do all of them like they haven’t been solved yet. Think till you either come up with the solution or are weeping profusely.
If I could go back in time I’d be more consistent for longer durations in my DSA journey, and wouldn’t stop giving CF contests for hackathons.
Don’t do what your friends are doing. Pick friends that are doing what you want to do.
Only pick the CS journey if you're passionate about it. If you’re not and you still have to pick it, then convince yourself that you’re passionate about it.
being a jack of all trades actually helped me in this round. I was able to answer any questions that came up, in terms of tech stack.
If they aren’t in your resume, you won’t be asked about them. But if they are, and you can answer the questions, that leaves an impression because it shows your passion.
For interviews my advice will always be to stop preparing answers. Ad lib. Improvise.
don’t be stressed about placements. It’s better to feel less happy when you’re finally placed, than to feel more sad every time you’re rejected.
walk into your first test assuming it’ll take 50 more of these before you’re finally placed. Make these tests/interviews feel like a chore, not a burden.
Also get CTC out of your mind. You young as hell. Think about the work you’ll get to do, that’s way more important.
Be genuine, and explain with thorough examples. Your aim is to convince them of your answer’s sincerity, not just tell them your answer.
smile.
Always walk in with a bright smile and a “how are you”. Don’t be a drag and just walk in and sit. Shake their hand. Lighten up the environment. Ask them about their day.

developing the skill of ad libbing answers to these questions. Preparing “scripts” for intros, personal questions, even project questions kills your flow and the interview’s vibe. It’s meant to be a fun conversation. Don’t make it boring or dull for the interviewer or yourself.
When you get something wrong, be graceful about it. Make a joke about it. Keep the interview light and always keep a classy, genuine smile up throughout.
If that happens, drink some water or something to give your brain time to get back to normal.
Go through each and every single previous year experience from ‘24, ‘25 and this year’s. They’re the most efficient revision you’ll get.
Just make sure they get to know you’re truly passionate about CS.

rounds.name: Online Assessment
rounds.description: On-campus online assessment conducted on HackerRank, consisting of three questions: two DSA-based and one SQL.

questions.text: Slowest Key – LeetCode: Given a list of keypress logs as pairs (key, time), where key is an integer from 1 to 26 representing lowercase letters (1 → 'a', 2 → 'b', ..., 26 → 'z') and time is the cumulative time (in seconds) when the key was released, determine which key took the longest to press. The time taken for the first key is time[0], and for each subsequent key is time[i] - time[i-1]. Return the character that took the maximum time. It is guaranteed that this key is unique.

Distance Between "programmer" Substrings: Given a string containing exactly two non-overlapping occurrences of the word "programmer", possibly separated by arbitrary characters, determine the number of characters strictly between the first full "programmer" from the left and the last full "programmer" from the right.

Time and Amount Aggregation with Joins: The question involved 2–3 tables and tested a strong understanding of JOINs, GROUP BY, and aggregations. It required summing durations in seconds and converting them to HH:MM:SS format using functions like SEC_TO_TIME, as well as converting cumulative amounts into billions.
Find user IDs of users who have ordered products from more than one category.
For each category, find the product that was sold the most (by total quantity ordered).
First Non-Repeating Character
Climbing Stairs
Encapsulation in OOP
Indexing in databases
With AI advancing rapidly, what is the role of a developer today?
Difference between a database and a data warehouse
What an alternate key is
Would you choose expensive infrastructure to reduce server load time, or stick to a budget and accept slower performance?
What I knew about MSCI
Whether I'd be open to working in a different domain or department

tips.text: A strong intro is important—it sets the tone and flow of the interview. Practice it in front of someone beforehand, to make it smooth and confident.

In college or hackathon projects, we often neglect the feasibility and scalability aspects. It's still important to have a basic theoretical understanding of these, even if you don’t have practical experience

Don’t overlook the HR round. Be well-prepared with common HR questions and think through different scenarios in advance. You won’t have much time to recollect answers during the conversation, as this round often tests your spontaneity and presence of mind
Placement is 30% luck, 70% smart work. Focus on what you can control—be well-prepared when the opportunity comes.
Give contests and mock interviews even if you feel underprepared. They help you assess your level and improve.
Don’t fear early failures; better to fail in practice than in interviews.
Focus on one company at a time, give your best, and if it doesn’t work out—learn, move on, and stay resilient.
Research the company thoroughly—memorize key facts & values but also understand their meaning and relevance to your profile.
Soft skills are crucial. Even if my answers weren’t perfect, I spoke with confidence, used technical terms, and explained with clear, relatable examples.
For almost a month, I reviewed past interview experiences and practiced answering questions out loud, refining them for clarity and impact

tips.text: Start DSA preparation early on. Try to consistently practice at least 1–2 questions every day. I personally followed Striver’s SDE Sheet, which is very well-structured and covers most interview-relevant topics.

Always try to solve questions yourself first. If you're stuck, watch the video explanation but make sure to code it yourself afterwards. Keep revising important questions and try to identify and remember common problem patterns across topics.
I started with the basics of Java. Here's a link I referred to: https://youtu.be/eIrMbAQSU34?si=_Vq7MalRpZaXJsO9

For OOPs concepts, I followed Kunal Kushwaha’s playlist, which explains everything in a beginner-friendly manner. Additionally, I read articles on GeeksforGeeks, which helped reinforce key concepts like encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.
For RDBMS, I watched CodeHelp by Love Babbar’s one-shot video. It covers almost all the concepts required for interviews.

I learned the basics from W3Schools and practiced extensively on LeetCode. I completed all 50 questions from the SQL 50 list and also solved 10–15 additional medium/hard-level questions to get more comfortable.
For OS and Computer Networks, basic articles from GeeksforGeeks are more than enough. Focus on understanding concepts like process/thread, scheduling, memory management, TCP/IP, and HTTP.

In some interviews, you're asked to design systems like a Library Management System, Parking Lot, or ATM Machine using OOPs concepts. So, be prepared to design small-scale systems applying classes, objects, inheritance, and design principles. Practice dry-running a few systems beforehand.

Before every interview, research the company, their culture, products, and latest updates. This not only helps you frame better answers but also helps you ask relevant questions at the end of the interview, which leaves a strong impression. Prepare an introduction which basically summarizes your resume. Know your projects and your resume very thoroughly.
